summary: Proposes an algorithm that lets several DHCP servers share the load of answering clients without talking to each other. Each server can work out whether a request is its to handle. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If several helpers share one counter, each can follow a simple rule to know which customers are theirs, so they never need to ask each other.

questions: how to split dhcp clients among servers
how does dhcp load balancing work
what is pearson hash in dhcp
what is a hash bucket assignment
how do dhcp servers split clients
subtitle: A hashing rule that lets several DHCP servers split clients between them without talking to each other.

tldr.problem: When several DHCP servers hear the same client broadcast, they may all respond, or a relay agent may forward the request to all of them, which is inefficient.
tldr.mechanism: Each request is hashed with Pearson's hash into a value from 0 to 255, and each server is configured with the set of hash values it should serve. Only the server whose set contains the hash responds.
tldr.outcome: Servers can be set to take preconfigured, approximate shares of the client load with no exchange of information beyond initial configuration, and no changes to existing DHCP clients.

today: RFC 3074 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says the technique could be applied to other protocols with similar characteristics.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
DHCP clients contact servers by UDP broadcast, so a client DHCPDISCOVER may be received by more than one server. All of them may respond and the client chooses. A BOOTP relay agent typically forwards or rebroadcasts client broadcasts to all configured servers, so a similar inefficiency exists there.

The algorithm was originally devised to support a load-balancing optimization of the DHCP Failover Protocol. The authors later realized it could also optimize cooperating DHCP servers and the relay agents that forward packets to them. It uses a deterministic hashing algorithm, so each server can be set up to accept a preconfigured, approximate percentage of the client load.
sections.eli5: When many helpers all answer the same question, it wastes effort. This RFC gives them a rule so only the right one answers.

sections.title: Key Terms and the Probabilistic Approach
sections.content:
The RFC introduces a few terms. A Service Transaction (ST) is a set of client-server exchanges that leads to a server providing or denying a service, such as the DISCOVER/OFFER/REQUEST/ACK exchange. The Service Transaction ID (STID) is the attribute of a request used for load balancing. A Hash Bucket Assignment (HBA) assigns a set of hash values to a server. A Server ID (SID) designates a server, and in DHCP it is the IP address or DNS name. The Service Delay lets a server answer late instead of ignoring a client.

The approach is probabilistic, because it is nearly impossible to foresee which client will request service next. Over short periods the actual share a server handles will likely deviate from the desired share. As the number of requests grows, each server's share approximates its configured percentage.
sections.eli5: The rule is like flipping coins: over a few flips the result can look uneven, but over lots of flips it evens out to the shares you wanted.

sections.title: Choosing the Key and Dividing the Buckets
sections.content:
DHCP servers MUST use the Client Identifier option as the STID if it is present. If it is absent, the hlen field gives the length of the data to hash and the contents of chaddr are hashed. At most the first sixteen bytes of the Client Identifier or chaddr are used.

The STID is mapped to a hash value from 0 to 255. Resources are allocated by assigning a set of hash values to each server, and a server only services a request whose STID hash matches one of its assigned values. Any bucket not assigned to a server means some clients are entirely ignored, which in some scenarios may be desirable.
sections.eli5: Every client gets a number from 0 to 255 based on its ID. Each helper is given a list of numbers it looks after, and ignores the rest.

sections.title: Configuring Servers, Delay and Forwarders
sections.content:
For a server, an HBA SHOULD be a simple bitmap of 32 octets. The first octet covers hash values 0-7 and the thirty-second covers 248-255, with the least significant bit in each octet the smallest value. A set bit means the server MUST service requests that hash to that value. The RFC's example bitmap makes a server handle values 0 through 47 and 64 through 127.

The optional delayed service parameter lets a server that would not normally serve a request respond anyway after a configured number of seconds since the client first tried. Without it, the HBA is a strict serve or do not serve policy. A server SHOULD use the secs field of the request if it is not zero, or it MAY track repeated requests with the same transaction ID and use the elapsed time.

For a forwarding agent such as a BOOTP relay, HBAs MAY be pairs of Server ID and hash values, so the relay sends each request to the server responsible for its bucket. A request may go to more than one server, for example both members of a primary-backup failover pair.
sections.eli5: A server keeps a checklist of 256 boxes, one for each possible number. If the box for a client's number is ticked, the server helps. If a helper is slow, a backup can step in after a short wait.

sections.title: The Pearson Hash Function
sections.content:
All interoperable implementations MUST use the same hash function with the same table. The RFC gives a C implementation of Pearson's hash with a 256-entry mixing table of distinct values in pseudo-random order. The hash starts at the key length, then for each key byte, taken from the last to the first, looks up the table at hash ^ key[i]. It needs an array lookup and an xor per byte.

A second function, accept_service_request, computes the hash, picks the bitmap octet with (hash >> 3) & 31 and the bit with 1 << (hash & 7), and returns whether the server should service the transaction.
sections.eli5: The hash is a scrambling recipe that turns any ID into a number from 0 to 255. Everyone must use the exact same recipe, or they would disagree about whose turn it is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The proposal provides no security by itself and does not affect existing security. If HBA contents are sent over the network while configuring a server, that message must be secured against tampering, because tampering with an HBA could cause denial of service for some or all clients.
sections.eli5: If someone sneaks in and changes the checklist, some kids might never get served. So the checklist must be sent safely.

items.title: Key
items.text: Client Identifier option, or chaddr (length hlen), first 16 bytes at most.

items.title: Hash
items.text: Pearson's hash gives a value from 0 to 255.

items.title: Lookup
items.text: A 32-octet bitmap says which hash values this server serves.

items.title: Delay (optional)
items.text: A server may still answer after a configured number of seconds.
